extracted.intended_audience: attorneys authorized to practice before the USPTO, respondents in USPTO reciprocal-discipline proceedings, Office of Enrollment and Discipline staff, and counsel handling attorney-discipline matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO applies when determining whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state disciplinary adjudication under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d) (the Selling test), including the exceptions a respondent must prove to avoid identical discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline presumption (Selling test / 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall consider any timely filed response and shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that one of the Selling factors applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation mirrors Selling v. Radford (243 U.S. 46 (1917)). The Office will impose identical discipline unless one of the enumerated exceptions is shown by clear and convincing evidence. The decision-maker is not sitting as a court of review to discover errors in the originating proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deprivation of due process (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: The procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must demonstrate the lack of notice/opportunity to be heard by clear and convincing evidence. Challenges to the originating jurisdiction's rules or procedures are generally waived if the respondent knowingly and voluntarily consented to discipline (e.g., via guilty plea or consent judgment). The Office will reject due-process claims that were waived by a respondent's voluntary stipulation to facts and agreement to the sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: There was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The respondent must show by clear and convincing evidence that the state proceeding's proof was so weak that the Office cannot accept its conclusion. A stipulation or consent to the facts in the originating proceeding makes it especially difficult to show infirmity of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To succeed the respondent must show a meaningful disproportion or other extraordinary circumstance making the imposition of identical discipline unjust. Routine circumstances (for example, that the complaint was anonymous) or mere disagreement about the sanction will not ordinarily meet this standard, particularly where the respondent agreed the sanction was appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that practitioner was not publicly disciplined (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d)(iv))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the respondent can show that the alleged discipline was not in fact publicly imposed, that may prevent imposition of reciprocal discipline; the claim must be supported by clear and convincing evidence of the absence of public discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof (respondent must show exceptions by clear and convincing evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reciprocal discipline cases, it is the respondent attorney's burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal/USPTO review applies a narrow standard and does not function as a de novo review to find errors in the state court/subcommittee proceedings (citing In re Kramer, In re Friedman, In re Zdravkovich). The respondent's showing must be persuasive and meet the clear-and-convincing threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited conduct triggering reciprocal discipline (§ 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] practitioner shal not ... [e]ngage in any conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding by a state authority that the practitioner's conduct violated rules that reflect adversely on fitness to practice before the USPTO may be the predicate for reciprocal discipline under § 11.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising must not contain misleading statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney advertising or direct-mail communications must not include misleading content or characterizations (e.g., false impressions such as 'Our Final Notice', misleading addressee references like 'Re: JP Morgan Chase Bank', or labels that create a misleading urgency or official appearance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misleading presentation in the body, header, address block, or labels of an advertisement can support discipline for unethical advertising. The decision lists concrete examples from the offending mailer (e.g., 'Confidential', 'File Number LAA 06999', 'Loan Modification Notice') as misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required disclosure: notice if recipient already retained counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements must include the required language advising that if the recipient has already retained a lawyer for this matter, they should disregard the letter (the Guillty Plea cites missing the sentence: 'If you have already retained a lawyer for this matter, please disregard this letter;').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of statutorily or rule-required cautionary language in an advertisement is a violation of advertising rules and can form the basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required disclosure of how recipient's name/address were obtained
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements must disclose how the practitioner obtained the intended recipient's name and address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose the source of the recipient list is a violation of the advertising rules relied on in the discipline here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include lawyer's name responsible for advertisement content
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney advertisements must contain the name of the lawyer responsible for the content of the advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to identify the attorney responsible for content is a violation and may be disciplined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade name must not be misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: A listed trade name (e.g., 'Loan Assistance of America Law Firm') must not be misleading about the nature, affiliations, or scope of the legal practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a trade name that creates a misleading impression can be the basis for discipline under professional rules regulating advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely filing requirement for advertising review
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain jurisdictions require attorney advertisements to be filed for review before or simultaneously with dissemination; failing to timely file an advertisement for review is a rules violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Untimely filing (or failure to file) for required pre-dissemination review supports discipline; the decision cites the advertisement was not timely filed as a ground for reprimand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of consent/stipulation on defenses to reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent's voluntary guilty plea, consent judgment, or stipulation to facts and agreement that a particular sanction is appropriate waives many defenses to reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a respondent signs a consent judgment admitting violations and agreeing the sanction is appropriate, the respondent has effectively waived challenges to due process, sufficiency of proof, and sanction severity in the reciprocal forum. Case law supports that voluntary waiver in originating proceedings reduces ability to relitigate those issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO notice and response procedure (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director must issue a notice directing the practitioner to file a response with the USPTO Director within forty days of the date of the notice setting forth any facts the practitioner believes establishes a genuine issue of material fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practitioner is given an opportunity to respond and to submit additional information within the 40-day window; failure to submit additional information after such an order limits the practitioner's record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability and publication of disciplinary decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary decisions and notices of reprimand are made public and are published (e.g., in the Official Gazette and made available at the Office of Enrollment and Discipline's Reading Room).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and public notice are part of the disciplinary scheme and may be invoked in reciprocal discipline proceedings.
